latin.294: Frustra autem istas de corruptione originali quaestiones nostris opponit: non enim sunt pares, nec ullam prorsus probandi vim habent. Respondeo ad primam, Cur Adami corruptio moralis posteros potius infecit, quam corruptio posterorum inquinavit Adamum? quia corruptio moralis non aliter quam per generationem carnalem propagatur: sunt autem posteri Adamaeo geniti, non autem Adamus ab illis. Ad 2. Cur Adami peccatum in posteros necessario descendit, caeterorum patrum non ita descendit? quia peccatum Adami fuit mutatio finis ultimi, atque adeo universalem in Adami naturam corruptionem induxit: immundus autem non potuit non immundum, caro non carnem gignere. Peccata vero aliorum patrum, hujusmodi corruptionis causae esse non poterunt, cum jam esset in eis producta, sed effecta quibus ipsa sese exercuit, & conservavit. Itaque quamvis a proximis parentibus eam proxime traxerimus, tamen Adamo, ut illius primo autori & scaturigini ascribi debet.
latin.295: Ad 3. Cur Adami peccatum Caino nocuit, Caini peccatum Adamo minime nocuit? quia Adamus genuit Cainum, non Cainus Adamum. Ad 4. Cur primum peccatum nos potius corrupit, quam sequentia Adami peccata? quia illud naturam Adami corrupit, ista corruptionem jam factam consequuta sunt ut causam effecta. Ad 5. Cur Adamus ab illa corruptione liberatus est, quam sua actione sibi comparavit; infantes omnes, qui nihil mali egerunt, non liberantur? Liberatus est ab illius corruptionis reatu gratia justificationis, & ab inhaerentia poenarum gratia regenerationis, quia credidit & resipuit; credidit autem, quia fuit electus. Idem evenit aliis omnibus electis. Cur autem hic potius quam ille fuerit electus, alii causae quam liberrimae Dei voluntati, de suo quod vult facientis, tribui nequit. Genuit autem non secundum gratiam, sed secundum naturam, conceptus corruptos, sicut arte circumcissus gignit incircumcisos.
latin.296: Ad 6. Cur Christus justitia & sanctificatio nostra dicitur, Adamus non dicitur peccatum & corruptio nostra? Quia nulla alia justitia justificamur, nulla alia virtute sanctificamur, quam Christi. Itaque in eo omnis nostra justitia & sanctificatio quaerenda. Non possumus similiter dicere, nullo nos peccato damnari, quam Adami. Nam & multorum aliorum sumus rei, & ad universalem corruptionem, quam ab Adamo traximus, multos habitus, seu particulares ad certa objecta determinationes nimis saepe adjungimus, & illud ipsum Adami peccatum non est nostrum donatione, aut imputatione ut Christi justitia, sed ratione propagati ex eo vitii nobis inhaerentis, quod vim habet nos condemnandi, non quia est Adami, aut profluxit ab Adamo, sed quia natura sua vitium est legi Dei repugnans. Ejus pro Pelagio & Socino quaestiunculis respondi: nunc videamus quomodo respondeat nostris.
latin.297: GAR. Nobis certa responsio suppetit, imputationem primi peccati esse actionem Dei liberam & voluntariam, ex certo Dei consilio judicioque, non ex solius naturae ordine dependentem. Neminem autem fuisse Dei consiliarium, qui ea nosse, & de iis respondere teneatur, quae Deus in verbo suo revelare noluit. Sufficere nobis ipsius rei notitiam, omnes scilicet in Adamo peccasse, & ipsius reatum super omnes venisse in condemnationem, atque ita primum illud peccatum in omnes imputatione descendere. Rationes illius judicii penes Deum esse cujus viae sunt impervestigabiles, & eius judicia abyssus multa. Rom. xi. 33. Psalm. xxxvi. 7. PLAC. Si immediata imputatio primi peccati est actio Dei libera & voluntaria, ea nisi in Scriptura revelata fuerit, sciri non potest. Atqui non est in Scriptura revelata, neque ad eam probandam ullam vim habent loca a viro docto hic repetita, ut partim jam patuit, partim ex dicendis manifestum fiet.
latin.298: Deinde si est actio Dei libera, quo modo est actio Dei judiciaria? Liberam enim, opinor, intelligit, quae potest absque ulla justitiae aut legis violatione omitti. Quomodo ergo judiciaria dicitur, si eam a Judice neque lex, neque justitia exigit? Si nemo tenetur ea nosse, quae Deus in verbo suo revelare noluit, certe nemo tenetur illam imputationem nosse, siquidem, ut contendo, Deus eam non revelavit in verbo suo. Caeterum quaestionibus illis oppugno potissimum rationes, quae reddi solent, cur unum illud peccatum primum nobis omnibus immediate imputetur. Iis igitur renunciandum est, ac ad solam Dei voluntatem confugiendum, cui placuit illud unum, non alia, imputare, aut nostris istis interrogatis respondendum. Denique cum Deus nihil faciat nisi sapientissime, & justissime, & optime, si ejusmodi imputatio aut justitiae, aut sapientiae, aut bonitati repugnare videatur, quominus tribuatur Deo pia refugit conscientia, nec potest id a se impetrare, nisi, vel tollatur illa repugnantia, vel disertis Scripturae testimoniis, quae profecto nulla sunt, ad eam credendam aliquo modo cogatur.
latin.299: GAR. Neque tamen quaestionum nodi putandi sunt insolubiles. Itaque nunc secundo loco Erotemata singula consideremus. Quaeritur primo. Si Adam peccavit, ut caput generis, cur non puniri debeat ut caput? Resp. Adamo cum tribuitur capitis nomen, rationem haberi non tantum originis carnalis, sed etiam foederis universalis illius, quod in Adamo Deus cum humano genere iniit. Cum ergo peccasse dicitur ut caput, non tantum denotatur, eum fuisse principium radicale totius generis, verum etiam ea conditione constitutum fuisse generis caput & principium, ut quamprimum ab obedientia praescripta deflecteret, non ipse tantum peccati sui reatu obstringeretur, sed & posteros omnes reos efficeret, ac proinde poena dignos. Hoc est ergo peccasse ut caput, se & posteros ob peccatum illud reatu involvisse. PLAC. Ita nodus non solvitur, sed augetur alio nodo: Nam praeter liberam & voluntariam illam actionem, quae Deo sine Scriptura tribuebatur, ecce aliam, nempe foederis cujusdam universalis pactionem, de qua ne gry quidem in Scriptura; & quod deterius est, conditio fingitur Deo haud satis digna.

pass_a.294: Those original-corruption questions set against ours are not equal and prove nothing. To the first—why Adam's moral corruption infected posterity rather than theirs him: moral corruption spreads only by carnal generation, and posterity is begotten from Adam, not Adam from them. To the second—why his sin must descend and other fathers' not: Adam's sin was a change of the last end and so brought universal corruption into his nature; the unclean begets unclean, flesh begets flesh. Other fathers' sins could not cause that kind of corruption once it already existed in them; they were effects by which it exercised and kept itself. So though we draw it most nearly from nearest parents, it should still be ascribed to Adam as first author and spring.
pass_a.295: To the third—why Adam's sin hurt Cain and Cain's not Adam: Adam begot Cain, not Cain Adam. To the fourth—why the first corrupted us more than later Adam-sins: the first corrupted Adam's nature; the later followed as effects of corruption already made. To the fifth—why Adam was freed from the corruption his act brought, and infants who did no evil are not: he was freed from its guilt by justifying grace and from inherent penalties by regenerating grace, because he believed and repented—and believed because he was elect. So with all the elect. Why this one rather than that is elect can be credited to no cause but God's freest will doing what He will with His own. He begot, not according to grace, but according to nature, conceiving corrupt ones—as one circumcised by art begets the uncircumcised.
pass_a.296: Sixth: why name Christ our righteousness and sanctification, yet refuse to name Adam our sin and corruption? Only Christ's righteousness justifies and only His power sanctifies—so seek all that in Him. We cannot say likewise that Adam's sin alone damns us. We are liable for many other sins; we keep tacking habits and particular bent onto the universal corruption drawn from Adam; and Adam's deed is not ours by gift or by charging as Christ's righteousness is, but by the vice it spawned and that sticks in us—which condemns not as Adam's property or outflow, but as a vice that by nature fights God's law. Those Pelagian and Socinian needles I have answered; now for his replies to ours.
pass_a.297: GAR's sure line: first-sin imputation is God's free, willing act from settled counsel and judgment, not nature's order alone. No counselor of God is bound to know or explain what God left unsaid in Scripture. Enough that we know the fact—all sinned in Adam, guilt reached all for condemnation, so the first sin comes down on all by imputation. Reasons of that judgment rest with God; His paths cannot be traced and His judgments are a deep gulf (Romans 11:33; Psalm 36:7). PLAC: A free, willing divine act of immediate first-sin imputation is unknowable unless Scripture discloses it. Scripture does not; and the texts he recycles here do not prove it—as partly shown already, and as more will show.
pass_a.298: Again: call the act free—how then judicial? Free, as I read him, means omitable with no breach of justice or law. Then how judicial, if Judge, law, and justice do not require it? And if we need not know what God left unrevealed, we need not know this imputation—my claim being that Scripture never disclosed it. Those queries mainly strike the usual grounds for charging that single first sin to everyone at once. Drop those grounds and hide in bare divine will (pleased to charge this one only), or else answer the queries. Last: God acts only with supreme wisdom, justice, and goodness; if this charge looks to fight those, a devout conscience will not pin it on God unless the clash is cleared or plain Scripture—none exists—forces belief.
pass_a.299: GAR says the question-knots are not hopeless, and turns to each erotema. First: if Adam sinned as race-head, why not be punished as head? Answer: 'head' covers not only fleshly origin but the universal covenant God made in Adam with humankind. Sinning as head then means he was radical principle of the race and was set as head on this term: the moment he left prescribed obedience, not he alone would wear his sin's guilt—he would also render all posterity guilty and fit for penalty. That is head-sinning: wrapping himself and posterity in that guilt. PLAC: The knot grows, not loosens. Besides the unscriptural free act pinned on God, here comes another—some universal covenant pact without a letter in Scripture—and worse, a condition invented that little becomes God.

294: But he opposes those questions about original corruption to ours in vain: for they are not equal, nor have they any proving force at all. I answer the first: Why did Adam's moral corruption rather infect posterity than posterity's corruption stain Adam? Because moral corruption is propagated in no other way than by carnal generation: and posterity are begotten from Adam, but Adam is not begotten from them. To the second: Why did Adam's sin necessarily descend into posterity, and that of other fathers not so? Because Adam's sin was a change of the last end, and so brought a universal corruption into Adam's nature: but the unclean could not but beget the unclean, flesh not but flesh. Now the sins of other fathers could not be causes of this kind of corruption, since it was already produced in them, but effects by which it exercised and preserved itself. Therefore although we have drawn it most nearly from our nearest parents, yet it ought to be ascribed to Adam as its first author and spring.
295: To the third: Why did Adam's sin hurt Cain, and Cain's sin hurt Adam not at all? Because Adam begot Cain, not Cain Adam. To the fourth: Why did the first sin rather corrupt us than Adam's following sins? Because that corrupted Adam's nature; those followed corruption already made as effects follow a cause. To the fifth: Why was Adam freed from that corruption which by his action he procured for himself, and all infants, who have done no evil, are not freed? He was freed from the guilt of that corruption by the grace of justification, and from the inherence of penalties by the grace of regeneration, because he believed and repented; and he believed because he was elect. The same happens to all other elect. But why this one rather than that was elect can be ascribed to no other cause than the freest will of God, who does what He will with His own. And he begot not according to grace, but according to nature, conceiving corrupt ones, just as one circumcised by art begets the uncircumcised.
296: To the sixth: Why is Christ called our righteousness and sanctification, and Adam not called our sin and corruption? Because we are justified by no other righteousness, sanctified by no other power, than Christ's. Therefore in Him all our righteousness and sanctification is to be sought. We cannot similarly say that we are damned by no sin but Adam's. For we are guilty of many others too, and to the universal corruption which we drew from Adam we too often add many habits, or particular determinations to certain objects; and that very sin of Adam is not ours by gift, or by imputation as Christ's righteousness is, but by reason of the vice propagated from it and inherent in us, which has power to condemn us not because it is Adam's, or flowed from Adam, but because by its nature it is a vice opposed to God's law. I have answered his little questions for Pelagius and Socinus: now let us see how he answers ours.
297: GAR. We have a sure reply ready: that the imputation of the first sin is a free and voluntary action of God, from God's fixed counsel and judgment, not depending on the order of nature alone. And that no one was God's counselor, bound to know those things and to answer concerning them which God refused to reveal in His word. That it is enough for us to know the thing itself—namely that all sinned in Adam, and his guilt came upon all unto condemnation, and so that first sin descends upon all by imputation. That the reasons of that judgment are with God, whose ways are unsearchable, and His judgments a great deep. Romans 11:33. Psalm 36:7. PLAC. If the immediate imputation of the first sin is a free and voluntary action of God, it cannot be known unless it has been revealed in Scripture. But it is not revealed in Scripture, nor do the places repeated here by the learned man have any force to prove it, as has partly already appeared, and will partly be made plain from what is to be said.
298: Next, if it is a free action of God, how is it a judicial action of God? For by free he means, I think, what can be omitted without any violation of justice or of law. How then is it called judicial, if neither law nor justice requires it of the Judge? If no one is bound to know those things which God refused to reveal in His word, certainly no one is bound to know that imputation—if, as I contend, God did not reveal it in His word. For the rest, by those questions I chiefly attack the reasons which are usually given why that one first sin is immediately imputed to us all. Therefore either those reasons must be renounced, and refuge taken in God's will alone, to whom it pleased to impute that one and not others, or our interrogations must be answered. Finally, since God does nothing except most wisely, and most justly, and most well, if such an imputation seems to clash with justice, or wisdom, or goodness, a pious conscience shrinks from ascribing it to God, and cannot force that upon itself unless either that clash is removed, or it is somehow compelled to believe it by express testimonies of Scripture—of which there are in fact none.
299: GAR. And yet the knots of the questions are not to be thought insoluble. Therefore now in the second place let us consider the erotemata one by one. It is asked first: If Adam sinned as the head of the race, why ought he not to be punished as head? Reply: When the name of head is given to Adam, account is taken not only of carnal origin, but also of that universal covenant which God struck in Adam with the human race. When therefore he is said to have sinned as head, it denotes not only that he was the radical principle of the whole race, but also that he was constituted head and principle of the race on this condition: that as soon as he turned aside from the obedience prescribed, not he alone would be bound by the guilt of his sin, but he would also make all posterity guilty, and so worthy of penalty. This, then, is what it is to have sinned as head: to have involved himself and posterity in guilt on account of that sin. PLAC. So the knot is not loosed, but enlarged by another knot: for besides that free and voluntary action which was ascribed to God without Scripture, see another—namely the pact of some universal covenant, of which there is not even a syllable in Scripture; and what is worse, a condition is invented hardly worthy of God.
